processing: Made as other Chinese black teas are: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried. A newer floral-fruity version adds a light tossing of the leaf after withering, borrowed from oolong work.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this tea specifically. As in other Chinese tea regions, spring leaf is the most valued; Hanzhong's northerly, cool climate makes its season relatively late.
appearance_dry: Typical of Chinese black teas of its kind: dark, fine twisted strips, sometimes with golden tips.
taste_profile: Few tasting accounts exist; expect the rounded sweetness of a northern Chinese black tea, and in the tossed style a more floral, fruity nose.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for fine Chinese black tea. Water a little off the boil keeps delicate leaf from turning sharp.

vintage_note: Like most Chinese black teas of this type it is normally sold as the current year's harvest, with spring lots priced highest. It is best drunk within a year or two; no ageing tradition is recorded for it.
description:
Hanzhong Hong is black tea from Hanzhong in southern Shaanxi, a tea area better known for its greens. It is a small regional tea and you are more likely to meet it locally than in an export catalogue.

The interesting part is the newer floral-fruity version. Its makers add a shaking step, a technique familiar from oolong work, and that shaking is regarded as the key to the aroma.

The cup of that style is bright orange-red, sweet and mellow, with flower and fruit up front. Treat it gently: short steeps and water a little under the boil keep the perfume from flattening. Taste notes for the plainer style are scarce, so judge it by what is in your own cup.

When buying, ask which style you are getting and which year it was picked. Little is documented about grades, so the seller's specifics matter more than the name on the bag.
history:
Little is documented about when black tea making began in Hanzhong. Tea itself has a long record in the area, though the most sweeping local claims come from promotional writing and are hard to check.

The floral-fruity style is described in a 2024 paper in the journal China Tea, by authors from Hanzhong's tea industry centre and a Chenggu County extension centre, as an innovation on the area's traditional black tea.
